Lessons.Title: Graphs That Represent Situations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: interpret zeros, maximum and viable domain of a quadratic model describing projectile motion and compare representations of a physical situation, recognizing that graph features depend on context. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U06:L14 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/6/14/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/6/14/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source uses frog jumps and launches; our original example is a mathematical scenario only.

Original idealized soft-foam ball height h(t)=−2t²+8t+10 metres for elapsed seconds t from release. At t0 height10m, at t2 height18m (maximum), at t5 height0m (ground), while algebra also yields a negative root t−1 which is not part of elapsed physical time. The meaningful flight domain is 0≤t≤5; outputs are nonnegative on it.

Rearrangements: h(t)=−2(t−2)²+18 (vertex form) and h(t)=−2(t−5)(t+1) (factored form). Each is identical to standard form; vertex form displays max at t2, factored shows zero at t5 and at t−1, standard shows initial height h0=10. This illustrates selecting the most useful form for a question.

Student task: match three equations and a graph to a single fictional flight, explain why t−1 must be excluded, compare the height at t1 and t3, and critique a graph plotted below ground after t5. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for mathematical equivalence, accurate vertex/zeros, domain/units and contextual interpretation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Contextual root
KeyConcepts.Definition: A model zero may mean a landing time when the output is altitude.
KeyConcepts.Example: h(t)=0 at physical t5, not t−1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Maximum height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Downward-opening quadratic reaches maximum at vertex.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple forms
KeyConcepts.Definition: Standard, factored and vertex forms display different features of one function.
KeyConcepts.Example: At t0 h=10 from standard form.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check equivalent forms
WorkedExamples.Question: Rewrite h=−2t²+8t+10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Evaluate explicit first-party quadratic coefficients and check graph features via algebra.
Steps: All expand to same standard polynomial.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find height peak
WorkedExamples.Question: Find highest h(t) during flight.
WorkedExamples.Method: Evaluate explicit first-party quadratic coefficients and check graph features via algebra.
WorkedExamples.Check: h1 and h3 both16m by symmetry.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find ground time and domain
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve h(t)=0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Evaluate explicit first-party quadratic coefficients and check graph features via algebra.
Steps: Factored form gives t−5=0 or t+1=0.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating negative root as a recorded past flight time
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The model describes time after release.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Extending height below ground after landing
CommonMistakes.Correction: Stop graph at physical landing time.

SummaryPoints: Physical quadratic graphs require contextual domain and units.
Different forms expose initial height, maximum or roots.
The fictional flight reaches18m at2s and ground at5s.
Teacher reviews form choice and contextual graph validity.
